title: Hay or está? Finding your way around
topic: hay / está(n); prepositions and adverbs of place
why: After the simple prepositions, this lesson teaches you to get your bearings: hay to say what there is, está / están to locate a specific thing, and the expressions of place (cerca de, al lado de, enfrente de…). It's the essential foundation for describing your neighborhood or home, and for asking directions later in the unit.

Hay or está?

For “there is” and “there are,” Spanish has a single word that never changes: hay. To say where a specific thing is, it uses estar: está (singular), están (plural). It all depends on what comes next.

What comes nextExample
hayun, una, unos, unasHay un banco cerca. (there's a bank nearby)
haya number, mucho, poco…Hay dos farmacias en la calle. / Hay mucha gente.
haya noun with no article¿Hay pan? / No hay metro.
está / estánel, la, los, las, a proper nameEl banco está a la derecha. / Las llaves están en la mesa.

Two mistakes to avoid

  • “Hay el banco”: impossible. With the definite article, it's está: El banco está aquí.
  • Hay never goes plural: English switches from “there is” to “there are,” but Spanish says Hay dos bancos with the very same word.

The logic is the same as in English: “Is there a bank near here?” / “Where's the bank?” Questions follow the same split:

You're looking for…You ask
any bank at all¿Hay un banco cerca?
a specific bank¿Dónde está el banco de la plaza?
the restroom¿Dónde está el baño?
Hay un supermercado en la plaza. Está al lado de la farmacia.There's a supermarket on the square. It's next to the pharmacy.
", "

Saying where: cerca de, al lado de…

SpanishEnglish
cerca de / lejos denear, close to / far from
al lado denext to
enfrente deopposite, across from
delante de / detrás dein front of / behind
encima de / debajo deon top of, above / under, underneath
a la derecha (de) / a la izquierda (de)on the right (of) / on the left (of)
en el centro (de)in the center (of)
en la esquinaon the corner
todo rectostraight ahead
aquí / ahí / allíhere / there (near you) / over there

Watch out for de + el

Almost all of these expressions end in de. Before a masculine noun, don't forget the contraction: al lado del banco, cerca del metro, enfrente del parque. Before a feminine noun, nothing changes: al lado de la farmacia.

En: in or on

En means both “in” and “on”: Las llaves están en la mesa (on the table), La leche está en la nevera (in the fridge). Encima de is mainly for emphasis: on top, above.

With nothing after it, drop the de: El metro está cerca (the subway is nearby), but El metro está cerca de la plaza. English does the same with “near” and “close to.” In Latin America, “straight ahead” is often derecho; in Spain, it's todo recto.

La parada está enfrente del parque, a la izquierda.The stop is across from the park, on the left.
", "

The neighborhood and the home

To describe a place, you naturally alternate between hay (what there is) and está (where it is). Read this description of an apartment:

En el piso hay un salón, una cocina, dos dormitorios y un baño. El salón está a la derecha; la cocina está al lado del salón.In the apartment, there's a living room, a kitchen, two bedrooms and a bathroom. The living room is on the right; the kitchen is next to the living room.
En el salón hay un sofá y una estantería. El sofá está delante de la ventana.In the living room, there's a sofa and a bookcase. The sofa is in front of the window.

And the neighborhood

To…You say
ask if there's a shop¿Hay una panadería cerca?
ask where it is¿Dónde está la panadería?
ask how far it is¿Está lejos? / ¿Está cerca?
answer with a distanceEstá a cinco minutos a pie.
say there isn't oneNo hay panadería en esta calle.

Notice está a cinco minutos: distance is marked with a, where English says “five minutes away.”

With no hay, the article is often dropped: No hay farmacia, No hay metro. It's just like English “there's no pharmacy.”
